explanations.answer: The key to the pit of the Abyss
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. John, who is seeing this vision, says the star "was given the key to the pit of the Abyss." Notice the star is handed the key. I once searched my whole bakery for a timer that was ticking right behind me, so I respect anybody who knows where the key is.

explanations.answer: A golden censer full of incense
explanations.explanation: A golden censer does show up earlier in Revelation, when another angel has one (Revelation 8:3), but that's not what the star gets here. In this verse the star is given the key to the pit of the Abyss. Incense smells lovely, but it won't open a pit. I've tried opening a stuck drawer with worse.

explanations.answer: A sharp sickle for the harvest
explanations.explanation: A sharp sickle does turn up in Revelation, but later on (Revelation 14:14), and not in this scene. Here the star is given the key to the pit of the Abyss. A sickle is for cutting and a key is for opening. Wrong tool for this job, friend.

That's right. The verse says "the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit." The smoke rises like the smoke of a great furnace, and it's big enough to darken the sun. My worst batch only darkened my mood.

This one is true, friend. John says "the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke from the pit." The smoke comes up like the smoke of a great furnace. So the smoke does darken both the sun and the air.

It's the other way around, friend. The locusts "were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree, but only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads." So the green things are off limits. You're right that real locusts usually go for the green, which makes this detail stand out.

Correct, the statement is false. The locusts "were told not to harm the grass of the earth or any plant or tree." They're told to harm only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads. Real locusts would have been eating the whole yard by now, but these ones follow instructions.

explanations.answer: Only those without God's seal on their foreheads
explanations.explanation: Yes. The locusts are told to harm "only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads." The ones with the seal are left out of it. The locusts only get the permission they were given.

explanations.answer: Only the kings and the mighty of the earth
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't name kings or the mighty here. It says the locusts were told to harm "only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads." What decides it is the seal, not rank or position. A fancy hat doesn't count, and I'd know, I wear a tall one.

explanations.answer: Only the people who live along the sea
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse is about where people live. The locusts were told to harm "only those who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads." The seal is what matters here, not the address.
The text says the opposite, friend. "The locusts were not given power to kill them, but only to torment them for five months." The power they get is to torment, and it has a limit.

That's right, false. The verse says the locusts "were not given power to kill them, but only to torment them for five months." It's a heavy part of the passage, and I won't pretend otherwise. The five months matter, because the time is set.

That's the word. "In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them." This is one of the heaviest lines in the passage. It tells how bad the torment is, since people long for death and can't find it.

The word in the verse is stronger than that, friend. It says, "they will long to die, but death will escape them." Rest is what you'd hope for after a long day. This verse is about something much heavier.

The verse doesn't say hide. It says, "In those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, but death will escape them." That's the word to remember here, and it's a heavy one.
You've got it. The verse says "the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle." A horse that's prepared for battle is armored up and ready to charge. That's quite a picture to get from a bug.

Plow horses are calm and steady, and the verse is nothing like that. It says "the locusts looked like horses prepared for battle." These are armored and ready to charge. A plow horse would have a few questions about this crowd.
A race horse is running for a prize, and this verse has something else in mind. John says the locusts looked like "horses prepared for battle." The picture is war, with no finish line in it.

That's right. John says the locusts "had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle." So there's iron-like armor, and a sound like a charging army. Imagine that coming at you in the morning when you're just trying to open your shop.

It's true, friend. The verse says they "had breastplates like breastplates of iron, and the sound of their wings was like the roar of many horses and chariots rushing into battle." Both the iron-like armor and the roaring sound are in the text. It's a lot to take in.
Exactly. The locusts "were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss." The verse gives his name in Hebrew and in Greek, and it's the same king either way. So these locusts answer to someone.

The prince of Persia is mentioned in a different book, Daniel (Daniel 10:13), and not here. In this verse the locusts "were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss." Wrong book, friend, though it was a good guess.
The king of the South is mentioned in Daniel (Daniel 11:5), not in this scene. Here the locusts "were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss." The title you picked belongs in another book.
Right. The verse says, "The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow." The eagle cried woe three times (Revelation 8:13), so one is down and two are left. The story is still going.
Close, but the eagle cried woe three times in all (Revelation 8:13), and one has already passed. The verse says, "Behold, two woes are still to follow." Three minus the one that's done leaves two.
Seven is the number of trumpets (Revelation 8:2), but the woes are counted separately. The verse says, "The first woe has passed. Behold, two woes are still to follow." So the number is two.

That's right. John says he heard "a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God." It's a golden altar, and it stands before God. The voice speaks to the sixth angel right after the trumpet sounds.

Golden lampstands are in Revelation, but earlier (Revelation 1:12), and not in this verse. Here the voice comes "from the four horns of the golden altar before God." The lampstands aren't part of this scene.

Golden bowls do appear in Revelation (Revelation 5:8), but the voice in this verse doesn't come from one. John hears "a voice from the four horns of the golden altar before God." So the missing word is altar.
That's what the text says. The four angels "were released to kill a third of mankind." This is a heavy verse, and the passage doesn't soften it. I'll say it plainly and keep my jokes out of it.
Sealing the servants of God is a different job, from earlier in Revelation (Revelation 7:3). These four angels are released "to kill a third of mankind." So that's the task in this verse.

explanations.answer: Gather the harvest of the earth
explanations.explanation: A harvest of the earth comes up later in Revelation (Revelation 14:15), but not here. The four angels from the Euphrates "were released to kill a third of mankind." It's a heavy verse, and that's what the text says.

Yes. John says, "the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number." He doesn't say he counted them, he says he heard the number. I'm sure he's glad someone else did the counting.
It's true, friend. The verse says, "the number of mounted troops was two hundred million; I heard their number." John heard the number. He doesn't say he counted.

That's right. The verse says, "The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions." The riders have breastplates in the colors of fire, sapphire and sulfur, and the horses have lion heads. That's a lot to take in at once.

No eagles in this verse, friend. It says, "The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions." The riders' breastplates are the colors of fire, sapphire and sulfur. Eagles will have to wait for another passage.
The verse doesn't mention oxen. It says, "The heads of the horses were like the heads of lions." So the answer comes straight from the text: lions.

That's the word. The verse says, "their tails were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm." The horses are dangerous at both ends, the mouths and the tails. I'll stay far away from the back end of any horse, thank you.

Scorpions are in this chapter, but on the locusts, whose tails had stingers like scorpions (Revelation 9:10). The horses are a different case. Their tails "were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm."
Eagles aren't in this verse. It says the horses' "tails were like snakes, having heads with which to inflict harm." The tail picture here is snakes, and I'll leave the eagles up in the sky.

explanations.answer: They cannot see or hear or walk
explanations.explanation: That's right. John says the idols "cannot see or hear or walk." These are idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood. They were made by hands and can't do a thing for the people who bow to them.

explanations.answer: They were carried off to Babylon
explanations.explanation: The verse says nothing about Babylon here. It says the idols "cannot see or hear or walk." An idol that can't walk wouldn't get far on its own anyway.

explanations.answer: They were broken in the earthquake
explanations.explanation: There's no earthquake in this verse. John describes the idols as things that "cannot see or hear or walk." That's all the text says about them.
The text says the opposite, friend. "Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft." The survivors don't turn away. It's a sobering verse.

Correct, the statement is false. The verse says, "Furthermore, they did not repent of their murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, and theft." That's a sad ending for this part of the story, and the text doesn't soften it.
